title: Her Senegalese great-grandmother and the songs she passed down
summary: Her great-grandmother was brought from Senegal at eight, remembered her father's name, and sang songs for the children; Paraco translated the language.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Your grandmother, was she in Santo Domingo? Was your grandmother in Santo Domingo also?
No, my grandmother wasn't from Santo Domingo My great-grandmother, my great-grandmother Was from Senegal
Senegal See, with Senegalian That's how we knew so many of them songs, you see And just now, because I want to remember my kids
Well, did they ever talk about a language called Wolfe or Jollof Or tribe or whatever you say?

Well, you see, she was my great-grandmother Was only eight years old when she was brought here So she don't remember, but very little She remember her father's name, Drosin Prince Prince Drosin Prince was his name And her mother then was called Zaire But her, she was only eight years old when they brought her here To the Senegalia in Africa, ain't it? On the border of the French, somewhere around there And they had an old man in the yard, they called Paraco He was the only one that spoke that Senegal language And he would translate it to her master But I don't remember my great-grandmother, you know
You don't remember any songs that they had?

Oh yes, oh yes Do you remember any songs? I used to Because my great-great-grandmother My great-grandmother Well, then she knew her mother would show her some of the songs That she could remember from her home And she'd sing it to us children
If you remember some of those, that would really be something extraordinary
If you could remember some of those, that would really be wonderful
Right now, if I wasn't I'd remember them all And sing them all, sing all the time I tell you, I sing all the time
